source.title: Deforming the Loss Surface to Affect the Behaviour of the Optimizer
source.authors: Liang-Ming Chen; Long Jin; Xiujuan Du; Shuai Li; Mei Liu

record.file_problem: Full paper and supplementary material supplied; no apparent cutoff affecting the reported experiments.
record.tranche_reason: Tests whether loss-surface deformation that changes optimizer trajectories also changes measured flatness and held-out image-classification performance, using VDMs rather than the claim versions' original interventions.
record.gate_note: The study reports VDM and learning-rate comparisons and flatness simulations/visualizations. Values in Tables 2 and 3 compare deformed with original CNNs; Table 1 compares learning rates and VDM settings. Simulated loss-surface results are not natural-data generalization results. It does not test random-label memorization, width sweeps, convolutional versus fully connected architectures, adaptive-optimizer comparisons, batch-size effects, dropout, magnitude-aware sharpness rankings, or removal of memorized examples.
record.test_reason: The study uses the premise that flatter minima can generalize better to motivate a loss-deformation method, then reports that method's accuracy and loss-curve visualizations. It tests none of V1–V8. In particular, filter-normalized loss curves do not establish V7's relationship between magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance and train–test error gaps among comparably fitted networks.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase broadly matches the authors' conclusion: theory, simulations and CIFAR-100 loss-curve visualizations suggest VDMs can filter sharp minima, and selected VDM configurations improve reported classification accuracy. Table 2's maximum CIFAR-100 gain is 1.46 percentage points for PreResNet-20, from 67.03% to 68.49%; ResNet-20 gains 0.91 points, despite the abstract attributing 1.46 to it. The authors acknowledge a flatness–training-loss trade-off and no single VDM working well everywhere. Their description of improvements as significant is unsupported by reported statistical tests.
record.recipe_differences: Adds a vertical deformation mapping to the loss during SGDM training; compares it with the corresponding original training recipe. Models use random crop and horizontal flip and standard cross-entropy training.
record.method_sensitivity: VDM family and coefficients change the result: some settings lower test accuracy, while most reported AP/LE settings improve it. The paper also states that excessive steepening can worsen performance due to a trade-off with training loss. The loss-curve visualization reports flatter minima with larger a1 or e2 for the tested settings.

fits_no_version.finding: Selected VDM settings improve reported accuracy across Tables 2–3; Table 1 also contains settings that reduce accuracy.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Loss-dependent deformation during momentum-SGD training can improve held-out image-classification accuracy, with outcomes depending on the deformation and its coefficients.

fits_no_version.finding: Figure 5 shows flatter filter-normalized loss curves for selected VDMs. AP (10, 1, 2, 1) is flatter than AP (18/π, 1, 2, 1), but has higher training loss and lower test accuracy, 69.19% versus 70.67%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: VDM-induced flatness can trade off against training fit; flatter visualized minima need not yield higher test accuracy when training losses differ.

record.problems: No uncertainty estimates or significance tests are reported for the accuracy comparisons. CIFAR results are medians of 5 runs, but individual run variation is not given. Flatness evidence includes loss-curve visualizations and simulated two-parameter surfaces; it does not directly measure the train-test error gap for the claim versions.
record.rows_left_out: None. Rows include the original-model reference values alongside each VDM comparison and the separate Table 1 VDM settings.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting versus natural-label held-out accuracy under the same architecture and recipe.
Generalization as width increases beyond the width required for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected classifiers and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under limited or broader tuning; recovery through weight decay or optimizer switching.
Batch-size comparisons under fixed epoch budgets and adaptations that remove their penalty.
Dropout comparisons, training-set-size dependence, excessive dropout, and joint removal with weight decay.

Magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance versus train–test error gaps among similarly fitted networks, and ranking against norm- and margin-based measures. Figure 5 supplies normalized loss-curve visualizations, not these measurements.
Retraining after removal of highly memorized examples versus equally many random examples.

record.verdict_notes: All rows remain linked to none; cannot_determine refers to their inability to establish a claim-version effect, not unreadable accuracies. Own-method comparisons and standalone reference values should be excluded from the claim-evidence rows. The paper cites batch-size and sharpness findings but supplies no batch-size experiment. Its flatness–accuracy trade-off does not challenge V7, which concerns similarly fitted networks and a specified gap measure.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label fitting and held-out natural-label performance under the same recipe.
Width sweep beyond the interpolation threshold.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and learned local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD and the effects of tuning, weight decay, or optimizer switching.
Large versus small batches under fixed epoch budgets and recipe adaptations.
Dropout addition/removal and its interaction with training-set size or augmentation.
Magnitude-aware perturbation sharpness and comparison with norm- or margin-based measures.
Removal of highly memorized examples and subsequent test accuracy.
